title: Blackout
excerpt: A blackout is when you drank so much that you can't remember anything about it later.
example: "I remember walking into the third bar. After that it's a total blackout."
text: During a blackout your memory simply stops recording. You still walk and talk, but nothing sticks. It is a clear sign you had way too much. Someone who got that drunk says they "blacked out". If a friend is in a bad state, don't hesitate to call an ambu.

title: Bodem leggen
excerpt: Bodem leggen means eating a proper meal before you start drinking, so you don't get drunk as fast.
example: Before the borrel started, he quickly ate a plate of pasta to bodem leggen.
text: It literally means "laying a foundation". The idea is simple. With a full stomach your body takes in alcohol slower. That lowers the chance of a hangover, or worse, a barf. Smart move before pre-drinks.

title: Body count
excerpt: In slang, body count is the number of people someone has had sex with.
example: "During the game someone asked what everyone's body count was. It suddenly got very quiet."
text: Body count started out as a military term for the number of dead. On social media it is about sexual partners. A lot of people think the question is rude, or that the number doesn't matter at all. Dutch students keep score with tijgerpunten.

title: Bottoms up
excerpt: Bottoms up is a toast that tells everyone to empty their glass.
example: "To the birthday girl! Bottoms up!"
text: With bottoms up the bottom of your glass goes up. So you drink it all. It is a lot like the Latin "ad fundum", where the Dutch adtje comes from. People shout it at birthdays or at the start of a night.

title: Bouncer
excerpt: A bouncer is the security person at the door of a club or bar.
example: "The bouncer looked at his trainers and said he wasn't getting in tonight."
text: The bouncer checks your ID, keeps an eye on the dress code and keeps things safe inside. Too drunk or acting up? Then you are out. Being a bit friendly to the bouncer almost always helps.

title: Brainrot
excerpt: Brainrot is the feeling that your brain is melting from too much dumb online content. The word also means that content itself.
example: "I watched TikToks for three hours and now I can only talk in memes. Total brainrot."
text: Brainrot was Oxford Word of the Year in 2024. Think of weird memes that get repeated endlessly and videos that make zero sense. People who doomscroll a lot often suffer from it.

title: Brak
excerpt: Brak is Dutch student slang for feeling hungover. Mostly the mental kind: tired, slow and good for nothing.
example: She spent all of Sunday lying brak on the couch, with just enough energy for Netflix.
text: Brak isn't really about headaches or nausea. It is the heavy head and the total lack of motivation. You exist, but that's about it. Some swear by a herstelbiertje to fix it.

title: Brassen
excerpt: Brassen is a ritual where two members of a Dutch student association grab each other by the collar to settle an argument.
example: They couldn't agree on who was right, so they decided to brassen it out in front of the sociëteit.
text: The winner gets a beer from the loser. The exact rules differ per city and association. In some places it is also called zooien. It is more tradition than fight.

title: Breadcrumbing
excerpt: Breadcrumbing means giving someone a little attention now and then to keep them interested, without really investing.
example: "Every few weeks he likes a story or texts 'hey'. Nothing else. That's breadcrumbing."
text: You are basically dropping breadcrumbs to keep someone on the hook. A flirty text or a like, but never a real date. It keeps the other person busy while you stay free.

title: Broke
excerpt: Being broke means you have (almost) no money left. Usually for a while.
example: "I can't come skiing, I'm really broke until my stufi comes in."
text: Broke is usually temporary and often said as a joke. At the end of the month a lot of students are broke. Someone who is always short on money is a broke student. The Dutch say skeer.

title: Broke student
excerpt: A broke student is a student who is always short on money and saves on everything.
example: "Store brand pasta and tap water. The life of a broke student."
text: The broke student is a stereotype all over the world. Rent, tuition and groceries add up fast. So students are always hunting for deals, free food and happy hours. In the Netherlands the free student travel card helps a bit.

title: Bs
excerpt: Bs is a Dutch abbreviation with a few meanings: from "boodschappen" (groceries) to Brightspace, the online learning platform of many universities.
example: "I'm going to do bs, do we still have milk?" she shouted through the house.
text: Most of the time bs just means groceries. But it can also mean Brightspace, where your course material and grades live. Or a Bachelor of Science. Context tells you which one. Groceries come from the super.

title: BSA
excerpt: The BSA ("bindend studieadvies") is the binding study advice that decides if you can continue your programme after your first year.
example: With a negative BSA she had no choice but to look for another programme.
text: Don't get enough credits in your first year at a Dutch university? Then you get a negative BSA. That usually means you have to stop and can't sign up for that programme again for a few years. So it is wise to keep up from day one.

title: BTW
excerpt: BTW stands for by the way.
example: "Great party yesterday. BTW, you left your jacket at our place."
text: You use it to quickly add something extra to a message. Fun fact for internationals: in the Netherlands BTW is also the word for VAT, the tax on everything you buy. So don't be confused when you see it on your receipt.

title: Bucket list
excerpt: A bucket list is a list of things you want to do at some point in your life.
example: "Skydiving has been on my bucket list for years. This year I'm doing it."
text: The name comes from "to kick the bucket", which means to die. A bucket list is full of trips, adventures and challenges. Lots of students make one for their student years.

title: Bueno
excerpt: Bueno is Spanish for good or okay. Dutch students use it to say something is fine.
example: "Bueno, let's just chill at my place tonight," she suggested.
text: Students drop it into Dutch sentences to say something is fine or settled. Usually without speaking any more Spanish than that. It is part of a little family of borrowed words, like vino and tranquilo.

title: Burger
excerpt: Burger (Dutch for citizen) is student slang for someone who no longer studies and works full time.
example: "Next year I'll just be a burger too," he said, half proud and half sad.
text: After your student years you become a burger whether you like it or not. A full-time job, your own place and commuting to the office by car or by burgerrups. It has nothing to do with hamburgers.

title: Burgerrups
excerpt: Burgerrups is Dutch student slang for the train that workers take to the office every day.
example: Every morning at seven he got on the burgerrups to the office.
text: It literally means "citizen caterpillar". A nod to the packed rush-hour train crawling along with all the office workers inside. Students watch it with pity. Until they join it.

title: Burner account
excerpt: A burner account is an anonymous or temporary account, so nobody knows who is behind it.
example: "Someone has been leaving mean comments under her posts for weeks. It's a burner account without a photo."
text: People use a burner to watch, post or comment anonymously. Sometimes to stalk, sometimes to troll. Unlike an alt account, a burner is meant to hide who you are.

title: Burnout
excerpt: A burnout is total exhaustion caused by long-term stress, often from work or studying.
example: "After months of studying, working and being on the board she was completely done. Her doctor called it a burnout."
text: With a burnout you are physically and mentally empty. Rest doesn't seem to help anymore. More and more students deal with it because of pressure to perform. Take the signs seriously and talk about it in time.

title: Bussin
excerpt: Bussin means something is really tasty or really good. Mostly about food.
example: "That kapsalon from the snack bar at three in the morning? Bussin."
text: Bussin comes from African American English and blew up on TikTok. You mostly use it for food, but also for music or a party. Want to say it even stronger? Then it is bussin bussin. A kapsalon, by the way, is the legendary Dutch late-night snack of fries, shawarma and cheese.

title: Buying a round
excerpt: Buying a round means paying for drinks for the whole group.
example: "I passed my exam, I'm buying a round!"
text: In the pub people usually take turns buying a round. That way everyone pays about the same. Whoever never buys one gets noticed fast. It also works great as the stake for an anytimer.

title: Bv
excerpt: Bv stands for "bestuursvergadering", the board meeting where the board of a Dutch association discusses everything going on.
example: The bv ran until after midnight because of a discussion about the lustrum.
text: During a bv the board talks about everything. Money, plans, problems and the next ALV. They happen every week. And they are rarely short.

title: Bvo
excerpt: A bvo, or bvo'tje, is a beer for on the way to a party or the soos. Short for "biertje voor onderweg".
example: Cycling to the soos, she had already put a bvo'tje in her water bottle.
text: Perfect for the bike ride or the train to a party. That way the night starts before you even arrive. It is pre-drinks, but mobile.

title: BYOB
excerpt: BYOB stands for bring your own bottle (or booze). You bring your own drinks to the party.
example: The invite said it clearly: BYOB, because the supply was gone.
text: You put it on an invite when everyone brings their own drinks. Maybe the host doesn't know what people drink. Or there is just no money to buy drinks for everyone. Very student.

title: Campus
excerpt: A campus is the grounds of a university, with lecture halls, student housing and other facilities.
example: "Let's meet at the coffee place in the middle of campus after the first lecture."
text: On a campus you find lecture halls, libraries, sports fields and often student housing. In the Netherlands Twente and Wageningen have real campuses. In most Dutch cities though, the university is spread across town and students live in student houses.

title: Cancel culture
excerpt: Cancel culture is when lots of people drop someone after they said or did something hurtful, often through social media.
example: "After those old tweets came out, the influencer was cancelled within a day."
text: With cancel culture people stop following, watching or buying. Sometimes companies pull out too. Supporters see it as a way to hold people accountable. Critics think it goes too fast and too far.

title: Cancelled
excerpt: Being cancelled means lots of people turn against someone after behaviour they find hurtful or unacceptable.
example: "He said something stupid on a podcast and was cancelled within a day."
text: Getting cancelled can be anything from a few angry comments to real consequences. Losing followers, sponsors or work. Among friends it is also a joke: "You don't like pizza? Cancelled."

title: Canon event
excerpt: A canon event is an experience that is part of your life story, even if it is embarrassing or painful.
example: "Your first hangover during intro week? That's just a canon event."
text: The meme comes from the film Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. There, canon events are moments that always have to happen. Online you use it for mistakes everyone has to make once. Like falling for the wrong person.

title: Cap
excerpt: Cap means a lie or an exaggeration. No cap means the opposite: I really mean it.
example: "He says he chugged twelve pints without stopping. That's cap."
text: Cap comes from African American English and blew up through hip hop and TikTok. Someone who lies is capping. With "no cap" you say you are telling the truth. Sometimes people just send a cap emoji.

title: Cappu
excerpt: Cappu is Dutch student slang for a cappuccino.
example: On the terrace she quickly ordered a cappu before the lecture started.
text: Next to the classic version with cow's milk there are oat, soy, coconut and almond ones too. Each with their own fans. A cappu before class is a ritual for half the students in the country.

title: Catfish
excerpt: A catfish is someone who uses a fake profile online and pretends to be someone else.
example: "All her photos were of some Instagram model. He just got catfished."
text: The term comes from the documentary and MTV show Catfish. A catfish uses photos of other people or lies about their age and looks. Sometimes as a joke, sometimes for money or attention. So always meet in a safe place first.

title: Chaotic
excerpt: Chaotic means messy, unpredictable and full of wild energy. Often it is meant as a good thing.
example: "Someone brought a karaoke set to the end-of-exams party. It was gloriously chaotic."
text: Online, chaotic is often a compliment. A chaotic night gives you the best stories. A chaotic friend is funny and unpredictable. It is close to unhinged, but usually a bit kinder.

title: Cheers
excerpt: Cheers is what you say when you raise your glass. In British English it also means thanks.
example: "To the graduates. Cheers!"
text: With cheers you raise your glass and clink it with the others. In the Netherlands you say "proost". In the UK you also hear cheers when someone holds the door for you. Then it just means thank you.

title: Chlam
excerpt: Chlam is Dutch student slang for chlamydia, a common STI among students.
example: After a restless night he decided to get tested for chlam after all.
text: You mostly get it from unprotected sex and at first you often don't notice it. Getting tested is free or cheap at the GGD in many Dutch cities. And a condo helps you avoid it in the first place.

title: Chronically online
excerpt: Being chronically online means your opinions, humour and language are clearly shaped by way too much time on the internet.
example: "She knew within a minute who posted what about whom. Truly chronically online."
text: You say it about someone who knows every internet drama or sees everything as a meme. Also about discussions that are huge online but nobody cares about in real life. The advice that goes with it: touch grass.

title: Chug
excerpt: To chug means drinking something really fast in big gulps.
example: "Chug, chug, chug!" the whole table shouted when he started on his beer.
text: You can chug any drink, but at parties it is usually alcohol. The Dutch version is adten, or doing an adtje. The difference: an adtje always means finishing it in one go. Always drink at your own pace.

title: Clickbait
excerpt: Clickbait is a title or thumbnail that makes you curious enough to click, while the content often disappoints.
example: "You won't believe what happened next!" Of course he clicked. Classic clickbait.
text: Clickbait uses over-the-top headlines, exclamation marks and shocked faces. The goal is as many clicks and views as possible. It usually promises more than it delivers. Its angry cousin is rage bait.

title: Clout
excerpt: Clout is influence, fame or status, especially online. People with clout get lots of attention.
example: "He only does those crazy challenges for the clout."
text: Clout chasing means doing anything for views, likes and followers. Influencers with lots of clout can start trends. It is often used in a negative way, for people who act fake to get popular.

title: Clubbing
excerpt: Clubbing means going out to nightclubs to dance, drink and meet people.
example: "After dinner we're going clubbing. Dress code: black."
text: Clubbing is about the activity, not one specific club. The word is mostly British. A night of clubbing often starts with pre-drinks and ends at an afterparty or the snack bar.

title: Comfort food
excerpt: Comfort food is food that gives you a warm, familiar feeling, especially when you feel a bit down.
example: "After that exam all I want is my mum's stamppot. Ultimate comfort food."
text: What counts as comfort food is different for everyone. It often has to do with your childhood or home. Think of pasta, pancakes or a bag of crisps on the couch. For the Dutch it is often stamppot, mashed potatoes with veggies. It goes perfectly with a comfort show.

title: Comfort show
excerpt: A comfort show is a series you watch over and over because it feels familiar and relaxing.
example: "I'm stressed, so I'm watching Friends for the seventh time. My comfort show."
text: With a comfort show you already know what is going to happen. That is exactly what makes it relaxing. Lots of people put on their comfort show during stressful times, like exam week.

title: Commissie
excerpt: A commissie is a committee of members that helps the board of a Dutch association with one specific thing.
example: This year she is on the party commissie, together with four other members from her year.
text: A commissie supports the board with one area, like recruiting members, events or the bar. Most associations have dozens of them. Joining one is the fastest way to make friends.

title: Condo
excerpt: Condo, also called regenjas, is Dutch student slang for a condom.
example: "Do you happen to have a condo on you?" she whispered to her housemate.
text: It is the simplest way to avoid chlam and other STIs. Depending on the city or friend group you also hear connie. Or regenjas, which means raincoat.

title: Connie
excerpt: Connie is another Dutch slang word for a condom.
example: He always kept a connie in his wallet, just in case.
text: People use it interchangeably with condo. Which one you hear depends on the city or friend group you are in. Same thing, same job.

title: Constitutieborrel
excerpt: A constitutieborrel (cobo) is the drinks party where a new board of a Dutch association gets congratulated.
example: After the board change, the whole sociëteit was packed for the constitutieborrel.
text: During the cobo every board member stands in line and guests come by one by one to congratulate them. Boards from other associations show up in suits and bring gifts. It is formal, long and full of beer.

title: Content creator
excerpt: A content creator is someone who regularly makes online content, like videos, photos, podcasts or livestreams.
example: "She is still a student, but she already earns more as a content creator than from her side job."
text: Not every content creator is an influencer. With creators the focus is on making content. With influencers it is about their influence on followers. Many creators earn money through sponsorships and subscriptions.

title: Cooked
excerpt: Cooked means someone is in trouble, exhausted or has no chance anymore.
example: "I haven't read a single page for this exam. I'm cooked."
text: The exact meaning depends on the situation. You can be cooked after a hard workout or after a bad decision. A team that is 4-0 down is cooked too. Basically: it's over.

title: Core memory
excerpt: A core memory is a memory that feels so important or special that you will never forget it.
example: "Eating fries on the beach at five in the morning with the whole group. Core memory."
text: The term got famous through the Pixar film Inside Out. Online you use it for moments you think you will still remember years from now. Usually funny or cosy moments with friends.
